gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1014t:
Information Technology, GAO-05-1014T of September 14, 2005, gives Congress a progress check on the FBI's push to replace its aging computer systems. Much of the bureau's gear dates to the 1980s. New systems aim to join up case work across the bureau. The flagship Sentinel program seeks a modern case file system. It follows the failed Virtual Case File project.

GAO sums up its past reviews of how the bureau runs this build-out. It covers plans, staff skill, tools, and checks on cost and time. The bureau is gaining the skill it needs, GAO finds. Hard tests in each of those fields still lie ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1054t:
Health Care, GAO-05-1054T of September 29, 2005, argues that shared tech rules are the hinge for better U.S. health care. Medical errors and clumsy paper work raise costs and harm patients each year. Linked computer systems could cut both. Storms and terror threats add one more push: rescue and health teams need systems that can swap facts fast.

A House panel asked GAO to sum up its past reports on health tech rules. GAO does that and lists its past advice. It then tracks fresh steps by the Department of Health and Human Services. Firm lead from the top is still the missing piece.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-364t:
Coast Guard, GAO-05-364T of March 17, 2005, reads the Guard's fiscal year 2006 budget ask through the lens of past GAO work. The ask totals $8.1 billion. That is a rise of $570 million over the prior year. The Guard's load has grown: sea guard work swells, while old tasks such as sea rescue and fish ground care go on.

Three fields draw the eye here. One is the sea plan for home guard. One is feat across all tasks. One is the fleet swap, led by the Deepwater build of far-sea cutters and planes. The notes flag where Congress may wish to keep a close watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-414t:
Meeting Energy Demand in the 21st Century, GAO-05-414T of March 16, 2005, frames the strain on the fuel web that built U.S. wealth. Cheap, full energy fed the land's growth for a century. Use has near tripled in 50 years. The land holds 5 percent of world souls but burns about 25 percent of world energy each year. Demand could grow by about 30 percent in the next 20 years.

Signs of strain show in price spikes and grid stress. Harm to the land and air grows plain too. GAO gives its view on supply and on use. It lifts the key queries a House panel must weigh as it shapes new fuel law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-444t:
Care for troops badly hurt in Iraq and Afghanistan is the topic of testimony GAO-05-444T, given on March 17, 2005. More than 10,000 servicemembers had been injured in the two conflicts. The Department of Veterans Affairs made help for the worst hurt a top priority. GAO drew on three recent reports about job training, health care, and care for post-traumatic stress disorder.

VA and the Defense Department were working on a deal to share data on the seriously injured. For now, VA relied on local staff ties with military hospitals to learn who needed help. A joint screening tool with four questions helped spot PTSD risk. GAO found that recovery timing made job help hard to schedule. Poor data also limited VA's sense of its PTSD treatment capacity. The testimony shows where the handoff from military to VA care could break down.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-554t:
U.S. work to keep China's markets open and fair is updated in testimony GAO-05-554T, presented on April 14, 2005. Trade between the two nations keeps growing. The U.S. trade deficit with China reached $162 billion in 2004.  GAO summed up its recent findings and advice on China's compliance with world trade pledges and on guarding U.S. ideas abroad.

China's entry into the World Trade Organization brought broad duties to open its markets. GAO's recent work tracked how well U.S. agencies press for that compliance. It also covered the fight against copying of U.S. intellectual property overseas. A second thread dealt with trade remedies for firms hurt by unfair trade. GAO had already put a set of recommendations to the key agencies. The testimony pulls those threads together for Congress. It shows where U.S. efforts have bite and where they still fall short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-564t:
Paying for long-term care as the population ages is the strain traced in testimony GAO-05-564T, presented on April 27, 2005. Long-term care covers health, personal, and support services for people with disabilities. Medicaid pays for much of it, which ties the issue tight to state and federal budgets. As baby boomers age, far more people will need such care. GAO set out the budget pressure ahead and points to weigh in any reform.

Spending on Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security is set to press hard on the federal budget for decades. The same wave of aging will lift demand for long-term care sharply. States share the Medicaid bill, so their budgets face the same squeeze.  GAO argued that reform talks must face the size of the coming demand honestly. They must also weigh who should pay and what the public purse can bear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-574t:
The President's Management Agenda, a White House drive to fix federal management, is assessed in testimony GAO-05-574T, given on April 21, 2005.  The administration has used GAO's high-risk list to shape several of its government-wide drives. This testimony weighs the gains so far and the hard problems that remain across the agenda's planks.

The drive has done real good, GAO said. It raised the profile of management flaws and pushed agencies toward results that can be measured. Agencies have moved ahead in the areas the agenda covers. Financial reporting has grown faster and more timely. A separate drive targets improper payments, which run to tens of billions of dollars. Lags persist, though, above all at the Defense Department. Its books and business systems need a deep overhaul. GAO urged the budget office to press harder on those defense high-risk areas in the second term.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-654t:
Help for homeless veterans to find and keep jobs fills GAO-05-654T, testimony of May 4, 2005. Veterans Affairs estimates up to 250,000 veterans are homeless on any given day. The Labor Department's reintegration program funds local groups to train and place them. Spending rose from $9.5 million in fiscal 2000 to over $18 million in fiscal 2004, with over $20 million expected in each of the next 2 years. The department runs 79 grants.

Placement is tracked, but keeping a job is the harder test. A formal job-retention goal was still being built when GAO testified, ahead of the program's renewal debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-664t:
Old immigration agency troubles in new bureaus fill GAO testimony GAO-05-664T (May 5, 2005). When the homeland security department absorbed immigration work in 2003, enforcement split between border and interior agencies. GAO finds the same strains that plagued the old service: fuzzy roles, clashing priorities, weak coordination, and data systems that mislead. A merger of the two bureaus has been floated as a cure.

GAO counsels care. Reshuffling boxes will not fix missing groundwork. It lists tests for any fix: a sound management frame, systems that support it, and patience with a department-wide change still in its early years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-714t:
Building the Capitol Visitor Center is tracked in GAO testimony GAO-05-714T of May 17, 2005. The three-story underground center is the largest Capitol grounds project in over 140 years, meant to secure and teach visitors. The testimony takes up the Architect of the Capitol's handling of schedules and contracts, the cost outlook with its risks, worker safety, and the monthly reports owed to Congress.

Earlier GAO advice and the Architect's replies are scored. The stress falls on schedule discipline: slips in the sequence drive contract costs. Lawmakers get a plain account of where the dig stands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-754t:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission faces review in testimony GAO-05-754T, given May 26, 2005. The agency watches 103 commercial nuclear power plants. Safety fears rose after a long shutdown at an Ohio plant in 2002. Spent fuel also went missing or uncounted at three plants. GAO summed up 15 recent reports and named the shared tests the agency faces.

GAO credited steps that raised plant safety and security. It also listed work left undone. Security for sealed radioactive sources needs to improve, since such sources could feed a dirty bomb. Oversight of plant security needs strength. So do checks on funds set aside to close plants, fixes tied to the Ohio shutdown, and control of spent fuel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-784t:
Pension enforcement is the topic of testimony GAO-05-784T, given June 9, 2005. A labor agency guards the benefit plans of more than 150 million people. Those plans hold over $4.4 trillion in assets. Recent scandals showed how abuse by plan managers can hurt workers. GAO described the agency's enforcement plan. It also scored steps taken on past GAO advice, and the challenges that remain.

GAO found a strategy built on targeted probes. Regional offices have wide freedom to shape their cases. Tips from plan members remain the main source of leads. The agency opens about 4,000 probes a year. It also teaches members and sponsors, and runs a program where plan officials can fix faults without penalty. GAO credited many fixes, but said hard challenges remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-794t:
Pension funding rules are the target of testimony GAO-05-794T, given June 7, 2005. Big firms have ended pension plans with wide gaps between assets and promises. The federal pension insurer swung from a $9.7 billion surplus in fiscal year 2000 to a $23.3 billion deficit by September 2004. Weak firms held plans short by $96 billion. GAO summed up its report on the funding rules behind the strain.

GAO said the rules aim at both firm long-term funding and short-term flexibility. In practice, they let reported funding be weak, unclear, and hard to read. Most of the largest plans still look sound, GAO found. Risk spikes when a weak sponsor nears failure. GAO argued the rules could vary with a sponsor's strength. Fixing the rules is key to any full reform, it held.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-824t:
Risk-based budgeting at Homeland Security is urged in testimony GAO-05-824T, given June 29, 2005. Past GAO work warns of a long-term fiscal imbalance. It calls for a fresh look at the whole base of government. The testimony shows how performance budgeting can inform choices. It gives homeland security cases where the department tried to set an acceptable level of risk.

GAO said reexamining old programs can free funds for new demands. Tools from 15 years of reform laws can support that work. But the tools help only if agencies use them and Congress weighs their results. Performance budgeting sharpens debate on what programs deliver. It cannot settle clashes of values, GAO noted. Risk principles can help the department send resources to the highest priorities first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-834t:
Legacy airline costs are weighed in testimony GAO-05-834T, given July 13, 2005. Older big airlines have lost money since 2001. Two large carriers used bankruptcy and ended their pension plans. The federal pension insurer took a $9.6 billion hit. Plan members lost $5.2 billion in benefits. GAO gave early views ahead of a full report due later this year.

GAO found legacy carriers have not cut costs enough to match low-cost rivals. Losses reached $28 billion since 2001. Low fares and high fuel costs squeeze them hard. Critics claim bankrupt carriers drag the industry down. GAO found no clear proof they harm rivals on fares or capacity. Most bankrupt airlines do not survive: 160 filed since 1978, including 20 since 2000. The real harm lands on pension members and the insurer, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-844t:
Transition help for returning troops is the topic of testimony GAO-05-844T, given June 29, 2005. Reserve and Guard members now serve far more often overseas. A joint program helps troops adjust to civilian life. Three departments run it together. In fiscal year 2004, about 309,000 troops were eligible. About 38 percent were Reserve or Guard members. GAO drew on its May 2005 report for this testimony.

GAO found that delivery and attendance vary a lot. Guard and Reserve members come home and leave service within days. Most have no time for the full program, and few get job preparation. Attendance at the disabled members' part is unknown, since one department does not track it. Agencies have improved content for full-time troops. Serving those who demobilize fast remains the hard problem, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-894t:
Flood map updates are explained in testimony GAO-05-894T, delivered July 12, 2005. Floods cause more damage than any other natural disaster in the nation. Losses came to about $55 billion from fiscal years 1992 through 2001. Many flood maps are over 10 years old. They miss erosion and drainage shifts. The testimony rests on a March 2004 GAO report.

The agency plans digital maps built with better data and posted online. GAO listed three expected gains. Towns can zone and build more wisely in flood zones. Owners who must buy flood cover can be found more easily. Officials can site key infrastructure with precise risk data. At review time, though, the agency had not set clear standards for how much data each risk level needs. Management of the strategy needed that base, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-924t:
The Navy's DD(X) destroyer faces a progress check in testimony GAO-05-924T, given July 19, 2005. The stealthy ship is built to strike land targets and rule coastal waters. The first ship is expected to cost $3.3 billion. Two big decision points were near: a milestone review and a critical design review. GAO covered the challenges ahead, the risk plan, and what shortfalls would mean.

GAO found demanding goals and tight time frames. The ship must hit land targets up to 83 nautical miles away, a range and accuracy not yet reached in naval gunfire. A radical hull and deep automation add risk. The schedule runs design, development, and building at once. Ten test models are a sound risk step, GAO said. But testing runs into the building phase. Flaws found late could force redesigns, delays, and cost growth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-934t:
Guard forces at nuclear sites are tested in testimony GAO-05-934T, given July 26, 2005. Five energy sites hold weapons-grade nuclear material. A heavily armed force guards them. GAO asked how far the forces meet current readiness rules. It also asked what they must do to beat a larger threat. A revised threat standard came in October 2004, with a deadline of October 2008.

GAO found the forces generally meet key current rules. Shooting skill, fitness, gear, and training programs check out. Weak spots remain. No standards govern how often each officer must join mock attack drills, and sites do not track who takes part. Officers at all five sites reported radio problems. Of 105 officers GAO interviewed, 66 said radios were not always dependable. Meeting the larger threat will take prompt, joint action, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-994t:
The strengthened visa process returns in testimony GAO-05-994T, delivered September 13, 2005. Consular officers are the front line against entrants who would harm U.S. interests. In October 2002, GAO named flaws and urged fixes. This testimony covers a report issued the same day on steps since 2002. It also covers a July 2005 report on Homeland Security staff placed at consular posts.

The same-day report's title states the balance. The process has been strengthened. Further gains would come from added management actions by State and Homeland Security. The July report covered the newer security officers working beside consular staff abroad. Together, the two reports frame what has changed and what has not. The testimony gives Congress both threads in one short account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1004t:
An anti-piracy drive gets early observations in testimony GAO-06-1004T, given July 26, 2006. Fake and pirated goods harm consumers, firms, and the economy. In 2004, the administration launched a multi-agency strategy against organized piracy. GAO drew on a prior report and on live work. It first mapped agency efforts that came before the strategy.

The testimony then gives first views on how the new strategy is organized and what it has done. A third part covers border work to keep fake goods out of the United States. That work ties to one of the strategy's goals. As early observations, the findings are framed as a baseline. Readers can see what the strategy inherited and where its first steps point.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1094t:
Security in Iraq is the topic of GAO-06-1094T, testimony dated September 11, 2006. From fiscal years 2003 through 2006, U.S. agencies reported large costs for stabilizing and rebuilding Iraq. About 138,000 U.S. troops served with the multinational force there. Over three years security grew worse, blocking wider U.S. goals. The statement tracks security trends and progress in building Iraqi forces. It draws on Defense and State department reports.

GAO laid out hard questions for Congress. What conditions must exist before U.S. forces can draw down? Why did violence rise as Iraq met political milestones and fielded more trained forces? What new steps would the administration propose if current measures fail? The testimony offers no easy answers. It gives overseers a factual frame for judging strategy, cost, and the shift to an Iraqi-led security role.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1114t:
Paying for the next generation air traffic system is the question in GAO-06-1114T, testimony dated September 27, 2006. Air traffic could triple by 2025, and current methods grow less efficient each year. A joint office housed at the Federal Aviation Administration coordinates the multi-agency build. GAO covered four points: cost estimates, views on today's revenue system, other funding options, and debt financing for capital work. The testimony draws on FAA and joint office records and interviews.

Cost estimates for the new system carry deep uncertainty this early. Stakeholders praise parts of the current system, which taxes airspace users to fund FAA. GAO weighed other ways to collect revenue from users. Debt financing could speed capital projects, but it adds interest costs and risk. The statement helps Congress judge how to fund one of the largest technical undertakings in government.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1134t:
Voting help for military members abroad is reviewed in GAO-06-1134T, testimony presented on September 28, 2006. The close 2000 presidential election raised doubts about whether troops and their families overseas could vote by absentee ballot. The Department of Defense runs the Federal Voting Assistance Program to teach and aid these voters. In September 2001 GAO urged fixes for uneven help across the services. Congress later asked what had changed by the 2004 election.

GAO compared the program's efforts in 2000 and 2004. It checked which of its earlier recommendations DOD had acted on. It found expanded outreach, but hard problems remained. Ballots still failed for reasons such as missing signatures or bad home addresses. GAO had urged a sound method to gather national data on rejected military ballots. The program prepared a post-election survey of about 1,000 local election officials for that purpose.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-164t:
Plutonium storage and the cost of weak planning are the subject of GAO-06-164T, testimony from October 2005. Plutonium is highly toxic and could be used in a nuclear weapon, so it needs heavy security. The Department of Energy holds about 50 metric tons left over from weapons work. Some sits as contaminated metal, oxides, and residues. The department plans storage capacity at its Savannah River Site in case it consolidates the material there. GAO checked how much plutonium the site could take and how well it can watch stored containers.

Poor planning, GAO found, has tangled the consolidation effort. Questions hang over how much material the site can accept and store safely. Container monitoring capacity is a second weak point. Until the material reaches final disposal, safe storage is the only guard. The testimony presses the department to plan before it moves one of the most dangerous stocks on earth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-174t:
Structural flaws in the National Flood Insurance Program are detailed in GAO-06-174T, testimony from October 2005. Recent hurricanes, Katrina among them, strained the 1968 program hard. The Federal Emergency Management Agency runs the program inside the Department of Homeland Security. GAO drew on past work to explain the program's finances. It covered homes that flood again and again, and the duty of some owners to buy coverage. It also previewed a report on the agency's oversight issued the same day.

By design, the program is not actuarially sound. Premiums do not build reserves for long-term losses, partly due to subsidized rates. The 2004 hurricane season forced the agency to borrow $300 million from the Treasury. Katrina then pushed its borrowing authority to $3.5 billion. Repeat-loss homes are about 1 percent of insured sites but 25 to 30 percent of claim losses. Oversight sampling also lacked a valid method.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-234t:
Pentagon business reform is graded in GAO-06-234T, testimony presented on November 9, 2005. The Defense Department wastes billions each year through weak business habits, GAO has long reported. Eight of the 25 areas on GAO's 2005 high-risk list sit inside the department. The 2005 defense law set terms for its systems overhaul, including a full transition plan. The department also built a Business Transformation Agency to push the work. GAO shared early views on each front.

Base steps are under way, GAO said, but much remains undone. An agency office alone cannot change how the vast department buys, pays, and tracks. True change needs leaders who stay the course, sound structures, and plans with teeth. The testimony checks the new agency's promise against that bar. It also weighs early compliance with the law's demands. The stakes are plain: business waste drains funds from war needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-244t:
The levee system that failed New Orleans has its history told in GAO-06-244T, testimony from November 2005. Storm surge is the gravest threat to the region; it kills more people than any other part of a hurricane. Surges on the Gulf and Atlantic coasts can top 20 feet. The Army Corps of Engineers built the Lake Pontchartrain and Vicinity Hurricane Protection Project to shield the basin's lowlands. Congress first approved the project in 1965. Hurricane Katrina flooded much of the city and breached those levees in 2005.

GAO lays out the project's purpose and its 40-year history. It traces how the work was funded over that span. The testimony makes no recommendations. Its value is the record: what was promised, what was built, and how money flowed. The statement helps Congress judge whether funding and design kept pace with the known risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-374t:
Matching flyers against watch lists sounds simple, but the build was hard. On February 9, 2006, testimony GAO-06-374T covered the Secure Flight program. After September 11, 2001, Congress created the Transportation Security Administration. It told the agency to take over passenger prescreening from air carriers. Secure Flight was the system meant to do that job.

GAO tracked progress in building and managing the program. It checked work with key partners and factors that shape how well the system works. It also weighed effects on privacy and passenger rights. The warning is clear. Big management challenges could hurt the program's rollout. Readers get an early check on a sensitive system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-444t:
Counting the whole country in 2010 would lean heavily on new automation. On March 1, 2006, testimony GAO-06-444T reviewed two key Census Bureau acquisitions. One system would standardize and merge data from census forms and other reply modes. The other would support field data collection. Congress had asked GAO to check both projects the year before. GAO briefed staff on results in January 2006.

This testimony sums up that briefing. It gives the status of each project. It also grades the management skill behind each one. Important work to improve management remains to be done, GAO said. Readers get an early warning, years before census day.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-474t:
Gas pipelines in crowded areas must be checked for corrosion and other flaws. In testimony GAO-06-474T (March 16, 2006), GAO gives early GAO views on pipeline safety. About a dozen people are killed or injured in gas transmission pipeline incidents each year. A 2002 law requires checks on segments in about 20,000 miles of busy areas. Half of the first checks are due by December 2007. The rest are due by December 2012.

Operators must repair or replace flawed pipe. They must recheck segments at least every seven years. GAO reports early results on safety effects. It also notes steps to strengthen enforcement. The views are preliminary, with fuller reports to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-484t:
Jobless benefits reach millions, yet who gets them and what follows is uneven. GAO's GAO-06-484T testimony, delivered March 15, 2006, draws on three GAO reports on Unemployment Insurance. In fiscal year 2004, the program covered about 129 million workers. It paid about $41 billion in benefits to nearly 9 million workers. Workers now face a higher risk of long-term joblessness than in the past.

GAO reports how many workers ever receive benefits. It shows which types of workers are more likely to receive them. It reviews how many claimants get reemployment services and how they fare. GAO makes no new recommendations here. A dispute with Labor over data needs is noted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-564t:
For the third time in this slice, the Future Combat System's business case is tested. On April 4, 2006, testimony GAO-06-564T updated the case for the Army program. The networked family of systems would cost on the order of $200 billion with related programs. Defense planned investment in new weapons doubled in five years. Research and development costs kept growing 30 to 40 percent. The program must compete for funds in a tight fiscal setting.

GAO discusses the business case needed for success. It presents recent recommendations to the Defense Department. It also lists matters for congressional consideration. An improved business case is the key, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-574t:
Designing the next air traffic system is a planning job shared by seven agencies. In testimony GAO-06-574T (March 29, 2006), GAO gives early analysis of the Joint Planning and Development Office. Congress created the office in 2003. It coordinates the move to a next generation air transportation system. The current approach grows more inefficient and obsolete, GAO notes. The office sits inside the aviation agency but has seven partner agencies.

GAO reports early results from its ongoing study. It judges how well the office builds interagency teamwork. It checks how stakeholders are brought into planning. It also weighs the technical planning done so far. The analysis is preliminary, as the title states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-604t:
War wear on trucks and guns must be repaired or replaced, a task called reset. Testimony GAO-06-604T, given March 30, 2006, gives early observations on equipment reset for the Army and Marine Corps. Operations in Iraq and Afghanistan are wearing out equipment. Some gear is more than 20 years old. The Army requested about $13 billion for reset in its fiscal year 2006 supplemental request. Large future spending is likely when fighting ends.

GAO addresses how the pace of operations shapes equipping and maintenance plans. It covers maintenance effects of those plans. It also names challenges affecting the timing and cost of reset. The observations rest on GAO reports from fiscal years 2004 through 2006.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-614t:
Chesapeake Bay cleanup efforts are the focus of GAO-06-614T, testimony GAO presented on July 13, 2006. The bay is the nation's largest estuary, and Congress has called it a national treasure. Since 1983, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, the District of Columbia, and the Environmental Protection Agency have worked as partners to restore it. Their Chesapeake 2000 pact set 102 goals under five broad aims.

GAO told the House panel that the partners' measures were not linked well enough to judge overall progress. GAO said program reports did not clearly tell the public how the bay was doing. Federal agencies and states had spent billions of dollars, yet teamwork and management were uneven. GAO urged sharper strategies to guide the cleanup.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-694t:
Burning wood waste for fuel and products is discussed in GAO-06-694T, testimony GAO gave on April 27, 2006. The federal government has pushed forest thinning to cut the buildup of fuels that feed wildfires. Thinning yields woody biomass, small trees and brush that mills once had little use for. GAO visited several users of this material. GAO set out what shaped their choices and what their experience teaches.

Users weighed hauling costs, steady supply, and local markets for the material. Some burned it for heat and power, while others made products such as mulch or pellets. GAO said these cases offer practical insights for ongoing federal efforts to promote biomass use. The testimony links fire prevention work to rural economic gains when the waste stream finds buyers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-714t:
Federal contracting in disaster recovery is revisited in GAO-06-714T, testimony presented on May 4, 2006. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita had exposed deep flaws in the government's response across the Gulf Coast. Contractors played a growing role in emergency work, from debris removal to temporary housing. GAO examined what went right and wrong in disaster contracting. GAO also gathered examples of sound practice from federal, state, and private sources.

GAO found inadequate planning and preparation for the contracting needs a disaster creates. Agencies had not lined up contracts or staff before the storms hit. That gap forced rushed awards with weak price checks and oversight. GAO urged agencies to pre-position contracts and train staff in calmer times. The testimony lays out fixes meant to make the next response faster and cleaner.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-774t:
EPA grant reforms get a spoken update in GAO-06-774T, testimony GAO delivered on May 18, 2006. The Environmental Protection Agency has long struggled to manage its grants well. Grants make up over half of its budget, about $4 billion a year across 93 programs. Recipients include state and local governments, tribes, universities, and nonprofit groups. In 2003, the agency adopted a five-year plan to fix its grant system.

GAO told Congress that the agency had made important strides under the plan. It had widened the use of competition to pick the most qualified applicants. New policies also tightened the award process. But weaknesses in putting reforms into practice continued to hamper grant management. Accountability gaps remained in monitoring and results. The testimony mirrors GAO's full report on the same reforms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-844t:
Disaster aid fraud is priced in GAO-06-844T, testimony GAO presented on June 14, 2006. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita destroyed homes and displaced millions of people in 2005. The Federal Emergency Management Agency rushed aid through its Individuals and Households Program. Speed came first, and controls came second. GAO estimated how much of that aid was improper or possibly fraudulent.

GAO put the figure between $600 million and $1.4 billion. Payments went to people who did not qualify, at wrong addresses, or more than once. Some claims rested on false identities or rented mailboxes. GAO's estimate rested on data mining of the payment files. The testimony shows the cost of paying first and checking later. It pairs with GAO's full report on the same program controls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-864t:
Passenger screening by the security agency is questioned in GAO-06-864T, testimony GAO gave on June 14, 2006. After September 11, 2001, the Transportation Security Administration took over passenger prescreening for domestic flights. Airlines had done the job before. The agency's Secure Flight program would match passenger data against terrorist watch lists. People flagged by the match would face extra scrutiny. GAO updated Congress on the program's management.

GAO said management challenges remain for Secure Flight. The program had already passed through an earlier, failed design under another name. Privacy safeguards, data accuracy, and testing all demanded care. GAO's past work urged the agency to prove the system works before it goes live. The testimony keeps a troubled program under a bright light. It reflects years of GAO warnings on watch list screening.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-884t:
Hardrock mining cleanup debts left for others to pay are taken up in a GAO statement for the record, GAO-06-884T, dated June 14, 2006. Laws such as the Superfund law place cleanup costs on the parties that caused the harm. Some mining firms, though, had shut down or gone bankrupt.

The statement draws on GAO's August 2005 report on cleanup debts. That report gave the Environmental Protection Agency nine steps to cut the public cost of costly cleanups. The agency agreed with many of them and said it would study some more. Readers get a brief account of who pays when polluters vanish.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-904t:
How Community Development Block Grant funds are shared out is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-06-904T, dated June 27, 2006. The Department of Housing and Urban Development runs the program. A reform plan would use one formula and five factors to split the funds.

GAO spoke from work still under way on better ways to target the money. It drew on design rules it had laid out in 2005 testimony. Congress had asked GAO to explore other formulas for varied towns and cities. The testimony frames the choices at stake. It helps readers judge what a fair funding formula must do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-954t:
Fraud in disaster aid, and a frame to stop it, are laid out in GAO testimony GAO-06-954T, dated July 12, 2006. Aid for single households must move fast after a disaster. Speed can open doors to false claims and misuse of relief funds.

GAO gave Congress a three-part frame. First, block fraud with data checks, system edits, staff training, and field tests. Next, spot it with data mining, hotlines, and watch on how relief cash is used. Last, probe and charge those who cheat. The testimony is a design brief, drawn from GAO fraud work, for aid programs that must stay both fast and clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-974t:
Paperwork load on the public is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-06-974T, dated July 18, 2006. Americans spend billions of hours each year on federal forms and surveys. The Paperwork Reduction Act aims to trim that load while keeping the gain from each form.

The Office of Management and Budget must clear each collection and report yearly on the load. Agency tech chiefs must review forms first. GAO spoke on the 2005 load report and its past study, GAO-05-424. Rising load hours, GAO said, show the need for a new approach. The testimony names flaws in review, and two agency models that worked better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1024t:
Privacy work at the Department of Homeland Security is graded in GAO testimony GAO-07-1024T, dated July 24, 2007. The department's Privacy Office began with a first chief in April 2003, under the Homeland Security Act of 2002. Its duties include clearing privacy impact studies, and weaving privacy into department choices.

GAO spoke on its recent report on that office. It set legal duties beside office steps, papers, and acts. Headway has been made, the title states. Yet ongoing hurdles face the office. The testimony shows the strain of guarding privacy inside a security giant, where data use grows each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1044t:
Exit checks for foreign visitors remain unsure, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1044T, dated June 28, 2007. The US-VISIT program has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars each year. It logs set foreign guests at over 300 air, sea, and land ports. Finger scans and photos screen them against watch lists.

Entry checks are in place. Exit checks, which prove a guest has left, lag. GAO told the state of both parts. It reviewed how the Homeland Security Department has run past and future exit work. The testimony rests on eight past GAO reports, plus work in progress. Prospects for a biometric exit tool stay unclear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1064t:
Military supply chains, a high-risk field since 1990, get a fresh GAO view in testimony GAO-07-1064T, dated July 10, 2007. Spare parts and key goods shape how ready U.S. forces are. In 2005 the Defense Department set a plan to fix its chain, aimed at lifting the high-risk tag.

The plan planks are forecasting needs, tracking gear, and moving supplies. GAO weighed headway on those planks. It set out results from recent work in each field. It asked how chain work links to wider business reform at the department. It also took up logistics rule and strategy. Gains could grow, GAO said, with a tighter link to outcomes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1074t:
High-risk truck and bus firms, and how regulators chase them, are the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1074T, dated July 11, 2007. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration picks firms for safety reviews with a tool called SafeStat. It weighs crash rates and past safety breaches. Bad reviews can park a firm.

GAO gave early facts from a recent report, GAO-07-585, and near-done work. It asked how well the agency spots firms that later crash at high rates. It checked if reviews are full and even across cases. It weighed how the agency follows up on grave breaches. The work rests on data from 2004 through early 2006.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1084t:
Charities as federal partners are profiled in GAO testimony GAO-07-1084T, dated July 24, 2007. The nonprofit sector helps deliver public services in health, learning, and aid to people in need. The federal government leans more and more on such networks to meet national aims.

GAO drew a picture of the sector: its size, its mix, and its place in the economy. It told how and why the government partners with charities. It named points about that partnership that need more study. The work is early, built on expert talks, past research, and round tables with scholars and field staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1104t:
Air system funding, and bills to renew it, are weighed in GAO testimony GAO-07-1104T, dated July 12, 2007. The Federal Aviation Administration runs one of the safest air systems in the world. Strain grows as travel demand climbs. A joint office plans its next era form, called NextGen.

Current law for the agency, its trust fund, and its taxes ends September 30, 2007. Senate bill S. 1300 and House bill H.R. 2881 name varied income paths. GAO asked if the current funding shape can bear agency work, NextGen among it. It weighed picked parts of the bills. It flagged points that could move NextGen's total cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1124t:
Disaster loan delays after the 2005 Gulf hurricanes drive GAO testimony GAO-07-1124T, dated July 25, 2007. The Small Business Administration lends to homes and firms hit by disaster. Hurricanes Katrina, Rita, and Wilma brought a flood of need the agency had never faced. Worry rose over how long victims waited for aid.

GAO, acting on its own, wrote two reports on that reply. The testimony sets out hurdles the agency hit in giving timely aid. It traces what caused them. It lists steps the agency has taken since to be readier for the next disaster. Field visits and agency papers feed the record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1144t:
Long-term budget strain needs more open books and tighter controls, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1144T, dated July 25, 2007. Near-term deficits had eased: the fiscal year 2007 gap was set at $205 billion, down from a February guess of $244 billion. That sum counts Social Security surpluses, though. Without them the gap is $385 billion.

The true test is long-term, GAO argues. Health costs grow faster than the economy, and the baby boom group starts to retire on January 1, 2008. The testimony weighs a return to pay-as-you-go budget rules. It then moves past caps, to clearer books and process change, for a path that can last.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1154t:
State Department staffing and language gaps persist, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1154T, dated August 1, 2007, revisiting its August 2006 report on the same ground. In 2002 State launched the Diplomatic Readiness Initiative to close shortfalls in staff numbers and skills. The gaps had hurt work at posts key to the war on terror.

GAO tracked headway since that push. It set out how far staff gaps have closed. It weighed if gaps in foreign language skill among officers and other staff have shrunk. The work rests on staffing and language data, and talks with State staff. The title verdict from 2006 stands in 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1194t:
Budgeting by results can help face this century's tests, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1194T, dated September 20, 2007. Performance budgeting links funds to what programs achieve. A 1993 law, the Government Performance and Results Act, set that aim for federal work.

With a long-term fiscal gap in view, GAO has argued that results data can drive a hard rethink: what the government does, how it does it, and who does it. The statement tracks headway in use of performance facts for budget choices. It names hurdles that stay. GAO pledges to keep working with Congress and the White House on the shift.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1244t:
Women's Business Centers give training and advice to women who run or start companies. GAO shared early views on that program in testimony GAO-07-1244T, presented September 20, 2007. The Small Business Administration funded 99 centers with about $12 million in fiscal year 2007. Congress and the centers worried about shaky funding rules. Some also feared the centers might duplicate two sister programs, the Small Business Development Centers and SCORE.

GAO's early review found that centers faced deep funding uncertainty. Until 2007, centers got support for up to 10 years, then had to sustain themselves. GAO also looked at how the agency oversees the centers. On duplication, centers often served different clients than the sister programs. Several also coordinated referrals with them. But GAO said the centers lacked clear agency guidance on how to coordinate well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1264t:
A 2006 security breach put veterans' private data at risk across the country. GAO returned to that theme in GAO-07-1264T, testimony dated September 26, 2007. It covers the Veterans Affairs Department's effort to centralize its technology program. That realignment began in October 2005. GAO also reviewed the department's work to strengthen information security after the May 2006 incident.

GAO said the department had fully met only two of six critical success factors. It had top leadership backing and a governance structure in place. But it still lacked a single team dedicated to running the realignment. New management processes were falling behind their own time frames. That put the 2008 completion target in danger, GAO warned. On security, the department had started several fixes. Yet it had not finished 22 of 26 earlier recommendations from GAO and its inspector general.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-254t:
Wrong payments by federal agencies are larger than the official totals suggest. GAO explained the gap in testimony GAO-07-254T on December 5, 2006. A 2002 law forces agencies to estimate and report bad payments. The testimony rests on GAO's review of fiscal year 2005 reports from 35 agencies. It covers reporting progress, open challenges, and money clawed back. Recovery auditing was part of the review.

Some agencies still skip required reviews, GAO said. The fiscal year 2006 total omits 9 risky programs. Medicaid alone spent about $183 billion that year. Estimates for 9 other programs, worth about $389 million, lacked valid sampling. Guidance from the budget office names no common risk factors to check. Recovery audit reports also proved shaky. Figures conflicted between agencies, and contract payments got little review. GAO pressed for complete reporting so Congress sees the true scale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-464t: The public's right to environmental data was shrinking in 2007, and GAO's briefing says EPA actions could cut the information's availability. The testimony defends the public's files. The findings warn that the green data belonged to the people. The sunlight was being shuttered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-484t: Small businesses hit by the Gulf hurricanes needed better disaster help in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the SBA's response showed the gaps. The testimony grades the relief. The findings demand that the next storm meet a readier agency. The Gulf's businesses were still rebuilding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-534t: The tobacco billions got a state-by-state accounting in 2007, and GAO's briefing reviews how states spent the settlement payments from 2000 through 2005. The testimony follows the money. The findings ask whether the smoking money bought health or highways. The settlement money was burning a hole.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-644t: The watchdog introduced itself to Congress in 2007, with GAO's briefing explaining how it served lawmakers through oversight, insight, and foresight. The testimony makes the pitch with real pride. The findings show the auditor selling its own value, politely but firmly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-684t: The new postal law was a second chance in 2007 — GAO's briefing again frames the reform as the mail service's toolbox for hard times. The testimony inventories the options. The findings' question repeats: would the tools be picked up, or left to rust?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-724t: Federal transit perks were being gamed in 2007 — GAO's briefing says weak controls let workers cheat the commuter-benefit program. The testimony exposes the fraud schemes in detail. The findings' moral is simple: free train passes need turnstiles too, or the honest pay for the cheats.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-754t: The port-security law got its checkup in 2007 — GAO's briefing reviews selected pieces of the SAFE Port Act's rollout across the country. The testimony samples how implementation was really going. The findings ask whether the landmark law was truly delivering safer harbors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-784t: The air-traffic system of tomorrow was on the drawing board in 2007 — GAO's briefing checks the shift to the next-generation setup. The testimony tracks the transition milestones. The findings warn that the future of flight needed a surer flight plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-794t: Too many nursing homes were failing the frail in 2007 — GAO's briefing says a troubling share still needed sustained reform attention. The testimony keeps the spotlight where it hurts. The findings' plea is simple: the last years of life deserve first-rate care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-824t: Signing the poorest seniors into drug plans was a 2007 priority — GAO's briefing examines the enrollment of the dual-eligible in detail. The testimony tracks the sign-up drive's progress. The findings ask whether the neediest actually got their prescriptions covered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-884t: Miles of border with no eyes on them — GAO walked Congress through the gaps in 2007. Its teams showed how easily the empty stretches could be crossed, far from any fence or sensor. The briefing's blunt point: the border is only as sealed as its loneliest mile, and plenty of miles were lonely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-924t: Checking every hire's papers was easier said than done in 2007 — GAO's briefing says a mandatory e-verify system faced real-world hurdles. The testimony maps the implementation maze. The findings warn that the grand plan would live or die in the details.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-944t: Crop insurance was leaking in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the program needed steady work on integrity and sane costs. The testimony presses for tighter screens on payouts. The findings ask whether the farm safety net was catching farmers or just catching flies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-994t: Trade's casualties got a catalog in 2007 — GAO's briefing lists the full menu of aid for workers hurt by imports. The testimony walks through benefits and services on offer. The findings present the safety net for globalization's losers, item by item.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-114t: GAO briefed Congress in 2007 on the atom cops — the Nuclear Regulatory Commission — as talk of a reactor boom grew. The briefing sizes up the safety referee just as the game was about to speed up.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-124t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that rebuilding Iraq's ministries was hitting a wall: graft, ghost workers, and offices that could not spend their own cash. Billions in U.S. aid aimed to grow working institutions, but the soil was thin. The briefing marks the moment Washington faced that fixing a government is harder than fixing its roads.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-144t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that U.S. crime-busters had no clear orders for helping foreign partners fight terror. When allies asked for a hand with terror cases, American agencies were left to wing it. The briefing flags a hole in the terror-fighting toolkit — teamwork with no playbook.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-154t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that the must-do audits of Medicare's private plans were duds. The health insurers running the Medicare Advantage option faced yearly checkups — but the checkups barely dented the question of whether payments were right. The briefing asks if Congress was getting the watch it paid for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-174t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony raises alarms about energy derivatives markets — the complex financial contracts tied to oil and gas prices. GAO found that rapid growth and new trading patterns were raising questions about whether the Commodity Futures Trading Commission could still oversee the markets effectively. The testimony landed just as energy speculation was becoming a political flashpoint.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-194t: GAO told Congress in 2007 to run the terror watch list like it mattered: tighter boss-level watch, fewer holes in the screens, and wider use where it could help. The lists were not pulling their weight, and GAO said the gaps could let the wrong people through. The briefing pushes a simple creed — a watch list only works if people actually watch it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-224t: GAO gave Congress an early warning in 2007: the FDA could not keep up with inspecting drug plants abroad. As more pills came from overseas, the agency's foreign checks lagged far behind the need. The briefing fed a growing fear — that the world's medicine cabinet was filling up faster than anyone was checking what was inside.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-254t: Presented as testimony in 2007, this Government Accountability Office report examines federal protection of service members' employment rights — the laws guaranteeing that deployed troops can return to their civilian jobs. GAO found agencies had taken steps to enforce those rights but warned that no single office kept a clear view of the whole effort. The report recommends centralized visibility so returning troops don't fall through the cracks.

The testimony sharpened the message for lawmakers — that the nation's digital defenses were only as strong as their weakest sector plan.
